subject: baku
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: baku, the dream-eating tapir spirit.
Style: ukiyo-e woodblock print.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module depicting a baku, the dream-eating chimera spirit, rendered in ukiyo-e woodblock style, aiming for a few hundred lines with careful attention to the SDK's API to avoid errors, while sketching its hybrid elephant-trunk, rhino-eyed, ox-tailed, tiger-pawed design.

I'm mapping the color palette and motifs — indigo, vermilion, cream, black ink lines, seigaiha waves, kasumi clouds, flame curls — onto a tapir-shaped body with its characteristic cream saddle band, deciding to use the glow kit for the swirling dream-smoke bubble and sizing the creature at roughly 1.1 meters tall and 2 meters long, facing +Z.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: a hips root joint, then a spine chain running from hips through chest to shoulders, followed by a neck chain, with the tapir's barrel body and arched back translated into joint positions, while the baku variant gets a longer curled trunk, tusks, a mane, tiger-like paws, and an ox tail.

For the body mesh, I'm sweeping a path from rump to chest with a radius function to get the tapir's wedge shape (higher and bigger at the rear), skinning it to the spine chain and hips so the mesh deforms correctly with the skeleton.

I'll keep it simple with a spine chain running forward from hips and a tail chain running backward, with the body sweep skinned as a single bone whose path starts behind the hips so the hips joint owns the clamped start point. Rigid versus smooth skinning isn't critical here, so I'll just proceed with defining the body path points.

Now I'm working out radius values along that path for rump, mid-body, and chest, then scaling the overall body height so the belly sits around 0.42m with roughly 0.42m legs underneath for a sturdy tapir-like stance. For length, I'm sizing the body from rump to chest to head, considering whether to scale this heroic baku slightly larger than a real tapir.

I'm also settling on the ukiyo-e palette: cream paper, two shades of indigo, vermilion, gold ochre, sumi black, and a pale blue.

For the tapir itself, I'm painting the front and rear sections dark indigo/sumi with a cream saddle in the middle like real tapir markings, adding fine grain texture and a soft "bokashi" gradient blending from cream to blue at the saddle edges for that classic woodblock-print look.

Adding seigaiha wave pattern...

Writing the seigaiha ring logic...

I'm deciding to place the seigaiha pattern subtly on the indigo body areas (hindquarters, shoulders) using lighter blue tones against deep indigo, while keeping the saddle cream with fine wood grain and thin vermilion borders, and the belly pale, consistent with hand-carved ukiyo-e aesthetics.

I'll handle the seam by normalizing the angle to a 0-360 range and letting the saddle/mane coloring hide any visible discontinuity, keeping the wave pattern generic across body and legs. Now moving to the head shape — a wedge-like tapir skull with an elongated snout, blending in baku-style elephant trunk features.

For stylistic details I'm giving it lion-like flame mane, round ukiyo-e eyes with vermilion rims, tiger paws, an ox tail, and curly kara-shishi brows with indigo-and-white spiral forelocks instead of horns. I'm also working out the neck and head joint positions so the thick, crested neck connects naturally from the chest up to a forward-leaning head base.

Adjusting neck curve for a more heroic lifted posture, then setting up a local coordinate helper on the head joint so I can place decorative elements like eyes and brows relative to the head's forward/up/left directions.

For the head itself, I'm building the cranium from scaled sphere primitives with low-poly flat shading to get that stylized woodblock look, keeping world-axis orientation so the ellipsoid scale stays intuitive.

Now I'm defining the muzzle as a swept shape extending forward from the skull.

The nose becomes a drooping trunk inspired by tapir/baku anatomy—a five-joint chain curving down and curling upward at the tip in an S-shape, tapering radius, with a vermilion accent band and dark nostril dot at the cap. For the lower jaw, I'm positioning a separate joint beneath the head, aimed forward, built as a scaled frustum or ellipsoid.

Mouth and jaw get finished out separately: lower jaw ellipsoid sits forward and down, and I add curved ivory tusks sweeping up from both jaw and upper jaw sides for the elephant/baku feel. I'm also adding a dark red mouth cavity inside, posing the jaw open slightly to reveal that vermilion interior with white teeth for a kabuki-like effect.

Now for the ears, I'm shaping rounded tapir-like ears with cream rims and white tips, building them as flattened indigo ellipsoids with a smaller inner cream layer, possibly using an extruded outline for a smoother rounded silhouette.

Confirming the outline points trace a convex counterclockwise loop, then coloring the ear with a paint function that shifts from indigo to cream toward the tip based on height. Now moving on to designing the eyes.

For the eyes I'm sketching an ukiyo-e inspired look: a white almond-shaped sclera with thick black outline, a glowing gold iris with black pupil and tiny cream highlight, and vermilion kumadori-style eyeliner streaks sweeping outward like kabuki makeup to give the baku a fierce, theatrical face.

I'm now setting up two decals per side on the skull — the eye itself and the fanning vermilion streaks behind it — placing them with proper orientation and mirroring so the model's right and left eyes match correctly from the viewer's perspective.

Next I need to compute the exact decal position by projecting around the skull's surface using azimuth and elevation angles to get a precise surface hit point.

For the forehead, I'm planning a vermilion tomoe-style emblem placed centrally.

For the mane, I'm thinking kara-shishi curl-flame plumes along the neck and spine, using swirled indigo blades with white and vermilion tips as decal cards positioned along a sweep path.

Cards work well since they're cheap geometry, four triangles each. I'm sketching a mane texture design: an indigo flame-curl shape with light blue inner strokes and a vermilion tip, bold black outline for the ukiyo-e look. I'm also considering adding gold/cream mist cloud cards near the feet to evoke the baku as a drifting spirit, though I want to keep focus on the subject itself.

Since props should only appear where the brief calls for them, I'll skip standalone cloud elements but fold cloud-wisp motifs into the anatomy itself -- flame-like puffs at the ankles and leg joints, echoing how lion-dog spirit beasts traditionally have tufts at their limbs. I'm picturing vermilion/gold flame-texture cards ringing the elbows and hocks, plus maybe a glowing dream orb near the trunk tip with wisps spiraling outward, tying into the baku's dream-eating nature.

Rather than freestanding transparency effects, I'll attach a swept spiral wisp directly to the trunk tip, trailing up into a small glowing orb with a crescent-moon texture, so nothing floats disconnected from the body. The trunk curling upward works well to carry that wisp naturally into the orb above.
